utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two things, Your Honour. First, yesterday the letters of August the 1st, 1995, that I spoke of, letters sent by the accused to Izetbegovic and Mladic I said were in English. The accused challenged that. The Chamber will remember that I'm not in a position at present to provide documents, but I'm doing my best to ensure that they may be provided. Although I'm quite satisfied that the covering letter or a covering letter from the accused was indeed in English and that Belgrade translations in English were provided, I'm also now satisfied that there were indeed Cyrillic Serbian originals. I forecast they will be that were signed and so that point, insofar as it was at point all, goes. And I'll make the documents available if and as soon as I possibly can but these are matters outside my control. Second point: Yesterday, the extent of the re-examination on the accused's own tab 8 caused me some concern but I raised an objection and the Chamber ruled against me, but it set me to thinking as I heard the extent of the inferences the accused was inviting the Chamber to draw from the documents it did have what other materials might be available the better to assist the Chamber, and of course the United Nations website has a great deal of material that can be downloaded, and I simply inform you that we have, and we have available for you in case you should find it helpful small collections of papers, I think they're neutral on the issues between the accused and the Prosecution, culminating in a transcription of the session itself. It's not really an argument because it appears the decisions have already been made. A transcription of the session where the various countries concerned make speeches, as Your Honour will understand and be familiar with, and it's quite clear from those sessions that tab 8 was not referred to. Indeed, in light of what is in the last paragraph of tab 8 it would be very surprising if it was referred to. So that would appear to confirm the point that the document was not considered at the time of taking the vote and making the speeches. But also, in addition to that material should you want it, the transcription of the hearing, there are two telegrams and one letter sent by Yugoslavia to the council in the lead-up to the decision and perhaps a document of which you will have already heard, the earlier report dated the 26th of May of 1992 on original Security Council Resolution 752. So that material's all available for you. It's about that much reading if you're interested in looking at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice. Mr. Milosevic, to complete your re-examination of this witness. Bear in mind the witness has been here four days.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am bearing it in mind. Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said at one point that the Kosovo Liberation Army was an infantry of NATO, and you were asked on what basis you asserted that. I assume you remember that. Do you recall saying this? Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Here I have photocopies of newspaper articles, and this is Ramush Haradinaj's statement. He is allegedly the Prime Minister of Kosovo at present. The title is NATO and KLA, A Single Army. It says, "Soldiers and officers who arrived worked with us as if we were the same army." That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please put this on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, how does that arise out of cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that what he said -- what Mr. Jovanovic said has been brought into question; that is, that the KLA played the role of a NATO infantry, and I am asking on what basis he said this. He was unable to provide material evidence, but now here I have an article where the same Haradinaj says that NATO and the KLA were a single army. You can see it from this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who asked that question, Mr. Milosevic? Who asked that question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can recall, one of you gentlemen. I think it was Mr. Bonomy who put that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Deal with it as briefly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I hesitated to see what was coming. It doesn't seem to me that even if I had adopted as a challenge a question from the Bench on this topic that would make this material admissible, for it's simply and clearly the expression of view by someone else sent out through the newspaper. And in our respectful submission, and I repeat, I don't want ever to be seen to be trying to shut this accused out of the material he wants to put in if it's admissible. I recognise the problems of objections which regularly take more time than they save because of what follows from my initial objection, but the Chamber may recall that there were significant limitations placed on our adducing additional material in re-examination. I'm reminded, for example, of a rather material file we wanted to put in with Lilic in his re-examination, refused. In our submission, the Chamber should be conservative in the liberty it allows this accused to add material to all they have to deal with and will have nil or almost nil evidential value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It was a question that I had raised, and I will allow the accused to deal with it very briefly. Very briefly, and let's see whether the witness can say anything about the newspaper article. If he can't, then we will not admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson, but I really must draw attention to what Mr. Nice said. He says that whatever is said here is irrelevant. For him, it is irrelevant when he introduces completely meaningless tabs about the content of United Nations Resolutions which is treated as if it was confidential, and then you can see that everything was published in the newspapers even before this Resolution was passed, and then he says it's not relevant. This is all part of his mystification. Why should something be public if it can be confidential? That's his logic. And I think you should draw his attention to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ramush Haradinaj --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, do I not want this tit-for-tat, and the parties should try to refrain from raising objections which will only trigger further comments from the other party. Mr. Nice, I don't wish to hear anything more about it. I don't think any offence was done to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There was no offence, Your Honour, and can I explain? This is one of the problems the accused is facing through not taking legal advice. The legal basis for the adoption of the evidence, which will be well understood to Your Honours, is something that the accused seems to have missed, and it may be that if I can't help, maybe Mr. Kay can explain it to him at the interval.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kay, no doubt, will have heard that. Proceed, Mr. Milosevic. Let us move on. And how long do you plan to be with this witness? How much longer?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope not more than half an hour, Mr. Robinson, unless I'm constantly interrupted. I understand the reasons for these interruptions, so I don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The assertion you made here has been put forward by Haradinaj himself in a much more clear manner.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please put this on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is mentioned here that the Serbian forces had used force - Kijevo, Decani, Prilep are mentioned - and he says to usurp Kijevo and continue with Decani and Prilep. All this shows that they were the ones that were doing this and the police were not using force disproportionately, that they were simply responding to this. Things were being turned upside down. The Albanians were supposed to be attacking the Serbian forces wherever possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Milosevic please slow down. The interpreters cannot keep up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, are you aware that NATO and the KLA were a single army, as Haradinaj says?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of this for several reasons, some public, some not. And many of these reasons were published in books written by the former KLA leaders and in the writings of some Western newspapers, as well as an officer of the Albanian army in Albania who took part in the fighting and in organising the passage of the KLA from Albania into Kosovo in order to pull out soldiers of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to make the NATO destruction easier, to facilitate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, is that the sole source of your knowledge of that matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About the battle at Kosara? That's a village near the border between Albania and Kosovo and Metohija. There are many statements about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question you're being asked is in relation to the relationship between NATO and the KLA, and is your sole source of knowledge about that what other people have written? Because if it is, it seems to me a pointless exercise asking you about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are public matters, and even the sparrows on the roofs knew about them. The contacts between the KLA and NATO were very close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You are the foreign secretary of the country and we have you here and there are relevant things you can be asked about that were within your personal knowledge and you're being asked about what was in the newspaper.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the world papers wrote about the battle at Kosara and yet Albanians from Albania passed over into Kosovo and Metohija and that this action was synchronised with the NATO bombing. What further proof do you need, Your Honours, in order to be convinced of this? The Western press wrote about it extensively, and it's a fact that the KLA, on the ground in Kosovo during the bombing, had satellite Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. telephone connections at their disposal. They could only have received this from Western countries, nobody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you have explored this matter sufficiently. Move on to another issue for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we get the date of this newspaper article?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. It's on the ELMO now. You can take a look at the date. This is an excerpt from the book written by Ramush Haradinaj who wrote about how the war for Kosovo and Metohija was prepared. The previous page - would you please put it on the ELMO - where it says -- where it says quite clearly what he said, that NATO and the KLA are a single army. Thank you very much. It's the 9th of January, 1993. Excuse me. This was published on the 9th of January, 2003. So the facts are coming to light, and ultimately the truth will be clear to everyone. I do not know if you will be among those to whom the truth will become clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, proceed with your re-examination, otherwise I'll stop it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, are you aware that, according to United Nations documents, the KLA was supposed to be disarmed?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Resolution 1244, regulating the end of the war and the arrival of the civilian and military international mission on that territory, points out that the KLA must be demilitarised. Demilitarisation, in my view and in the interpretation of those who understand these matters, means disarming.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the KLA, which included all these murderers and criminals who even took photographs of themselves with severed Serbian heads, became the so-called Kosovo Protection Corps, and they remained under arms but only changed their name?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't answer. It doesn't arise out of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice said that I used, as he said, Serbian nationalism in order to further my career. Are you aware that in 1989 I was the president of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Or, rather, at that time the president of the Presidency of Serbia, and a year later, at these multi-party elections that took place, I became the president of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that in 1989 you were the president of the Presidency, a collective body, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that's the position I held when I spoke at Gazimestan and afterwards I was elected. So I was holding the top post in Serbia. Is that in dispute?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how could I have furthered my career? Where else could I have gone? How could I have been promoted?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not clear to me either, because you were already at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it isn't clear to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The accused's questions are probably valueless, and the answers, but he also doesn't accurately characterise the way I put the Prosecution case. I maintain, of course, that his assumption and retention of power is in answer to certain constituencies, and I express myself quite cautiously, carefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic; move quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, you were asked about the Cutileiro plan. In the negotiations on the Cutileiro plan, did anyone participate from Yugoslavia or Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In these negotiations which were organised by Ambassador Cutileiro, and he was told to do so by the Conference on Yugoslavia, were only three sides participating from Bosnia and Herzegovina without the presence of anyone from Yugoslavia, from Croatia, or from any other country outside Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a tripartite meeting, and only the three constituent nations in Bosnia and Herzegovina were present, and the negotiations were chaired by Ambassador Cutileiro. There was nobody else present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And those three sides agreed on their own, with Cutileiro's mediation, that the plan should be adopted before any kind of hostilities broke out. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This plan was called the document on the constitutional order of Bosnia and Herzegovina on cantonal principles, or something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please look at tab 22, which refers to the year 1993. I am interested only in one very brief excerpt towards the end, where it says all the blame is one-sidedly again being shifted onto the Bosnian Serbs, and this is given emphasis. "The condemnation of the Bosnian Croats is very mild although the Russians asked that the battles in Central Bosnia and Mostar be condemned, because at that time there was also a war between the Croats and the Muslims." So here, too, all the blame is being shifted onto the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry, this is all comment. If you look at tab 22, what the accused has just put onto the record, unless I'm missing it, is entirely his comment preparatory for a question. I don't make these objections often, but really he must be kept to comprehensible questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, ask a question and avoid the comments. Avoid the preparatory comments.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am afraid that there is a misunderstanding, Mr. Robinson, because what I read out is not a comment. It's a quotation from tab 22, a quotation. It says that all the blame is being -- "As a result of that, the adopted communique was not balanced, bias and on the front-burner they put the blame on the Bosnian Serbs." This is towards the end of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That having been clarified, what is the question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can it be seen from this document also that there was a continuous double standard approach? We saw in tab 8 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no. That's not permissible. Next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will reformulate my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, we saw yesterday when we analysed the Secretary-General's report and the Resolution introducing sanctions, that the report said that the KLA had withdrawn but the Croatian forces had remained in Bosnia. In the Resolution, sanctions were imposed on Serbia while the Croats were only mildly warned that they should withdraw their forces from Bosnia. In this telegram, we see that all the blame is being shifted onto the Serbian side while the Croatians are only given a very mild warning. Is this something that runs through the entire Yugoslav crisis?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The line taken by the United Nations towards the Bosnian Serbs was always more severe than towards the Bosnian Croats, not to mention the Bosnian Muslims who were almost never criticised. And this was something that constantly ran through the whole process. Whether this was a result of developments on the ground, it's hard to say, but it's true that there was pronounced hostility towards the Bosnian Serbs which ran through all these documents, while on the other hand the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims, when they fought among themselves, and they did so very cruelly at that time, this was never practically reflected in the documents, this tripartite civil war, and no appeals were made for this to end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, yesterday to Mr. Nice's question you said that you had read all these tabs. Perhaps you have. Perhaps you've read them in more detail than I have because I had less time. So please tell me this: Am I understanding it correctly, namely, that in all of these tabs pertaining to events mentioned in the contents of the Resolutions which deal with Srebrenica, do these documents constantly mention only Bosnian Serbs but not Yugoslavia? Did you find Yugoslavia ever mentioned in these documents?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring to the UN documents, then I did not find the mention of Yugoslavia in those documents, rather only the criticism corrected at Bosnian Serbs and their conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice said that you had to know on the 12th of July about what was going on, and he asked you about what steps you had taken in relation to this gravest crime, as he called it, which took place in Srebrenica. I will now show you the cable sent by Mr. Akashi on the 12th of July. I will not quote everything, but I will put it on the ELMO. This telegram, this cable is Exhibit 713, as is indicated in the upper corner. 28th of July, 2004 is the date when it was admitted. Therefore, you already have the document. On the 12th of July, therefore, Akashi writes at the end of the first paragraph: "There had been no reports of physical mistreatment."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we probably need a copy of this on the overhead projector, and it's not sufficient for the accused, with his characteristic disdain, simply to say that, well, you've got it, I don't need to do anything about it. If he's going to present a case, he's got to apply the practices and rules that accommodate the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I understand he's going to put it on the ELMO. Let it be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, you can see to your left, because what I marked with yellow highlighter may not be visible on the screen.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is visible. This sentence that I read out, "There have been no reports of physical mistreatment." This means that the United Nations, which had several hundred soldiers there from the Dutch Battalion, they also had their representatives, they had no reports regarding this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I will not allow that. That's a comment. What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, we will cover the chronology from that time on. Did it occur to anyone at the time that any crimes had been committed there?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no information. It had never occurred to me until much later, when they started discussing it and reporting it, first of all at the UN and also in the international media. However, immediately after the fall of Srebrenica, we had no information. At least, I had no Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. information that some terrible things had happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. It has been frequently mentioned here that in Bosnia and Herzegovina, not to mention Serbia, Yugoslavia, a policy of forcible expulsion was pursued as well as ethnic cleansing. You have mentioned several times what I suppose is known to everyone, that there were crimes committed and that there was violence on all three sides. I will now show you a document dated 19th of August, 1992. 1992. It has been translated into English. You can put the English version on the ELMO, and I will be reading out from the Serbian original [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] same text. [Interpretation] It says here -- I did not check the quality of the translation, but it should be good. So it says on the 19th of August, 1992, president of the Serbian republic, as it was called at the time, Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Radovan Karadzic, signed this document in August of 1992. This was sent to the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, Ministry of the Interior, and all security centres. And then it says: "In accordance with our document of the 13th of July, 1992, pertaining to compliance with norms of international laws of war, I once again reissue the order." And then I will skip over this bit where it says that everybody has to abide by the Geneva Conventions, especially the third and the fourth one, and I would like to draw your attention to point 3. Therefore, he orders that the "forcible expulsion of people and other illegal measures against civilian population be prevented. Any certificates on the selling of property or statements by refugees that they would not return have no legal validity and declared invalid." This is what is stated in the order by Radovan Karadzic. And at the end, it states the following: "The general position is that all police organs and all army organs --" or, rather, "all organs of the army and police in the area of responsibility are duty-bound to thoroughly investigate any cases where there's reason to believe that the norms of international humanitarian laws had been violated." It says in item 5: "All members of police of the Serbian republic have to provide all assistance to the representatives of the Red Cross, UNHCR, and other humanitarian organisations. Full security must be ensured for these persons as well as full access to all prisons where prisoners of war are held." Therefore, my question is as follows: This is in line with what we have heard from the leadership of Republika Srpska, and we have documents to confirm it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the question? I mean, this -- what you have read is an order prohibiting forced transfer. What is the question in relation to that order?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm on my feet. I also observe the question, I think, if I understood it correctly, took about four minutes to read out, three or four minutes. Not the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have taken an equally long time to read out --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sometimes, yes, Your Honour, but when there is no sustainable question at the end of it, it really is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us hear the question. Let's hear the question concerning this order.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is very simple, but this does not deal only with forcible transfer or expulsion. I would like to remind you, Mr. Robinson, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's hear the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, according to our information, did the leadership of Republika Srpska try and did it take measures to prevent this from happening, and did it punish the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We constantly received assurances from them that that kind of conduct was banned. I know about a year or so ago a book was published where all such instructions and orders by Radovan Karadzic were published, as well as his correspondence with international dignitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm not now speaking about the book which was published a year or two ago. I'm now referring to this order from August of 1992. Therefore, my question is very clear: According to our knowledge at the time, did the leadership of Republika Srpska try and did it in fact undertake measures in order to prevent any kind of an ethnic discrimination and to ensure compliance with Geneva Conventions and so on?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We received such assurances from them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I ask that this be exhibited because this is a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, one of the questions you were asked there was whether the Republika Srpska tried and took measures to prevent this from happening and did it punish the perpetrators. Can you give me an example of the punishment of perpetrators that you were aware of at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally am not familiar with all of the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Perhaps there were such cases in the course of the war, but I'm unable now to give you more details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It would appear all you're doing is confirming very, very leading questions put to you by the accused without having any personal knowledge of the circumstances at all, and it concerns me that these may well be valueless answers and valueless questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not present in Bosnia throughout the entire period of the war except that I was in Bijeljina on one night. Therefore, I was not kept abreast of the developments there. And you cannot expect me to say any more than what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My criticism is not aimed at you, it's aimed at the pointlessness of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, your last question. We must bring this to an end.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have several more questions, Mr. Robinson. I don't know why this should be my last one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I will only allow one more.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have several more questions. Are you not going to allow me to put them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You can put one more question and we'll bring it to an end.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. I will ask the next question that's on my list. It is very difficult now for me to distinguish between what is important and what isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at tab 51. This is the Secretary-General's report. I would like to draw your attention to the date of this report, the 30th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't have 51, Mr. Milosevic. We stop at 50.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's in the binder provided by Mr. Nice. These are Mr. Nice's papers, not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it was an existing exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, at the very beginning, it says on page 1, among other things, it says: "My Special Representative raised the issue in a meeting with President Milosevic..." It deals with the issue then. "Various efforts have been made by my Special Representative to obtain access for UNPROFOR --" therefore, access for UNPROFOR -- "to Srebrenica and Zepa ... My Special Representative raised the issue in a meeting with President Milosevic on [In English] 12 August 1995, in which he referred to the commitment made by General Mladic to General Smith on the question of ICRC access to the missing from Srebrenica. President Milosevic promised to do all he could to convince General Mladic to grant such ICRC access but indicated that he was having difficulties communicating with General Mladic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, were you at this meeting, the meeting between the representative and Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I was no longer minister of foreign of affairs at the time and that Mr. Milutinovic probably attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The dispatch sent on the 14th of August, so more than one month after the Srebrenica events. So this is the dispatch sent by Akashi. This is your Exhibit 714.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what is the question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to draw his attention to this dispatch, Mr. Akashi's dispatch sent to Annan at the UN, who at the time was under-secretary for operations, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He explains: "I suggested that recent allegations appearing in the press about human rights --" "[In English] I suggest -- I suggested that recent allegations --" [Interpretation] So he says, "I suggested --" this is in Akashi's dispatch sent to the UN on the 14th of August. I suppose that based on that this report was written. And at the end of the first paragraph of this dispatch, and I will put it on the ELMO: "[In English] I suggested that recent allegations appearing in the press about human rights violations made such access all the more important."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Put it on the ELMO and read it. Do it in an orderly way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this Exhibit 714 or 13? Can we see the upper part of the exhibit? Yes, 714.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, do you have personal knowledge of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, I was still holding the office of the minister. I was in that position for several more days after that. And if the telegram arrived while I was there, then, yes, I was aware of it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, what I'm trying to show here is that on the 12th of August, the events in Srebrenica were not known. And if we take a look at the UN Security Council Resolution at tab 57 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't want a speech. Just ask a question of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, does this document discuss at all and does this document provide any information about something grave having happened at Srebrenica? Did anybody know about this at the time?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew nothing about it. And this shows that Mr. Akashi didn't know anything about it either and that he was putting in efforts to learn Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. something more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, is it clear that even on the 21st of December, 1995, when the Security Council adopted Resolution 1034, therefore in December of 1995, this Resolution states: "Affirms that violations of humanitarian rights in the area of Srebrenica, Zepa, Banja Luka, Sanski Most from July to October 1995 must be fully and properly investigated [In English] by the relevant United Nations and other international organisations and institutions."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it is being said that an investigation is necessary, and this is being said at the time when international forces are only a month away from entering Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That corroborates what you are saying, namely that all these were rumours that needed to be confirmed by international factors. Nobody knew definitively that something had happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When we condemned the attack on Srebrenica, was our motivation that it was an attack on a UNPA, that it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That concludes the re-examination. Mr. Jovanovic, that concludes your testimony. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it, and you may now leave. We will exhibit the document which Mr. Milosevic wanted to have exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Karadzic's order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The order by Karadzic. You may now leave, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D279.

utterances.speaker: MR. OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is no need for me to stay here. It was a privilege and honour to represent my country here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you for your presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before the next witness is called, Mr. Milosevic -- did you have something to say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I have an observation to make, a complaint, rather. I believe it is completely justified, but it is up to you to judge. Yesterday during the examination by Mr. Nice, and several months ago when we had before us Witness Diego Arria, I believe his name was, both times, in a completely inappropriate manner, a document of the International Court of Justice on provisional measures was used. My complaint is that did you not reprimand Mr. Nice for the way he was using it, because the International Court of Justice did not go into the merits of the case, and he only made certain -- quoted certain claims made by Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have stopped that, Mr. Milosevic. If you had an objection to make about the use by Mr. Nice of the ICJ case, then you should have made the objection at that time. Before the next witness is called, I want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before the next witness is called, I want to use this opportunity to express the Trial Chamber's views and conclusions about the use of time by the parties. My first remarks are addressed primarily to the accused, and the second set of remarks will be addressed primarily to the Prosecutor. Mr. Milosevic, so far you have called 19 witnesses. Your recent witness list was a list of 27 witnesses. On your own estimate, these 27 witnesses would utilise 108 hours, and at four hours per day that would be 27 days. When that is added to the two-thirds of the time for cross-examination allotted to the Prosecutor, that would be 18 days and make a total of 45 days for these 27 witnesses. So far you have used 30 days. So that at the end of the examination of the list of 27 witnesses, you would have used a total of 75 days or half of the assigned period of 150 days, and in that period you would only have called 27 plus the 19 witnesses already called, making a total of 46. What is even more alarming is that the witness list, your recent witness list, comprises Kosovo witnesses so that at the end of 75 days or half the time allotted, on the most optimistic estimate, only one-third of the Defence case would have been presented. Now, I looked at the witness list, and I'm troubled by the time that you have set for some of these witnesses. Four hours for three witnesses. I mean that is each. For two witnesses, six hours each. For another two, seven hours each. And for another three, nine hours each, and for one witness, 12 hours. Is this the best use of the time given to you? And more significantly, more importantly, is this the best use of the Court's time? And we say no. At this rate, it is very likely that at the end of 150 days, no more than 100 or 110 or 120 witnesses would have been called. The Chamber makes it clear that you must bear, you will bear ultimately the responsibility for this, but we will monitor examination-in-chief carefully to ensure that time is properly used. Evidence must be relevant and must not be unduly repetitive. Now, Mr. Nice, the Trial Chamber's allocation of time was based on the expectation that, given your experience and professionalism, cross-examination would not take up more than two-thirds of the time used for examination-in-chief, but this premise has not been borne out in practice. Our statistics show that cross-examination has consumed as much as 80 per cent of the time for examination-in-chief. You're also introducing many documents in cross-examination, and this has the effect of lengthening the re-examination. You will attend to that, but the Trial Chamber will also be monitoring strictly the introduction of items in cross-examination. The Chamber brings these matters to the attention of all the parties, and this includes the assigned counsel. The Court's time must be used efficiently and well. We are not satisfied in particular, Mr. Milosevic, that your use of your time is the best use of that time, and hereafter, we intend to be very strict but fair in monitoring the use of the time allocated to you. We're keeping the use of the Court's time under review. We are not satisfied with the pace of the trial. And I should say that in due course, one of the measures that we may very well have to consider is to seek the advice of the medical personnel as to whether the accused, who has been in good health for several months, can work for four days per week for three weeks per month. I also want to mention to the accused that he has an assigned counsel. The Appeals Chamber has illustratively listed some of the ways in which assigned counsel can be of assistance to the accused, and naturally the Trial Chamber's approach to the use of time must obviously take account of this facility which is available to the accused. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One observation. Of course we'll do all we can to ensure that the allotted period of time, two-thirds for both cross-examination and administrative matters I think was the original scheme, will be met or bettered, and indeed with the last witness I think I'm under 50 per cent of the time that he took by my cross-examination. The practice that I was able to introduce with this last witness of the pre-reading of Defence exhibits existing or new that I propose to ask a witness to deal with is one that it seemed to me bore some fruit with the witness because certainly on the second day he was able more swiftly to deal with propositions than would have been the case had he had to be taken through exhibits, and I would be grateful at some stage for being informed, if the Chamber feels it can, as to whether pre-reading is something the Chamber finds helpful particularly with an eye to judicial economy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It is helpful, but I think it is something to be addressed on a case-by-case basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. But looking at the witness list, we see several witnesses of the kind for whom pre-reading of some of the meetings, for example, will be very valuable, but we'll do our best to comply, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I mentioned the time that you have estimated for some of the witnesses; four hours, six hours, seven hours, nine hours, and for one 12 hours. You should try to aim to have a witness's testimony finished as quickly as possible. Do you really need that length of time for examination-in-chief? For some witnesses you have an hour and a half. I mean, that's fine. But I would say that you should aim to have a witness not spend more than a day in examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you said earlier that you would lead the evidence orally, not relying on witness statements. However, for the sake of time - I'm speaking for myself - I would like to advise you now to consider presenting some part of your evidence by way of written statements using the regime of Rule 89(F) or 92 bis. Take Danica Marinkovic, for example, who appears on page 3 of your witness schedule. According to the schedule, you are saying that you anticipate nine hours for your examination-in-chief. I understand that she's the judge who undertook the investigation into the Racak incident. I know that she's an important witness. However, I don't understand why you should spend nine hours or two and a half days only for your examination-in-chief while she has nothing to say about the acts and conduct of yourself. As a judge, I believe she must be capable of producing a written statement of what she had seen and experienced in a professional way so that you can concentrate in your examination-in-chief on important matters that should be dealt with orally and on introducing exhibits that should be tendered through her, substituting other peripheral matters with the written statement. In such a way, I believe you would be able to conclude your examination-in-chief in a session or two, saving much of your precious time. I advise you to bear this in mind in planning the future witness schedule.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may say something, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I would like to point out that your advice is useful indeed, and I will endeavour to make the most rational use of my time possible. However, I do believe you should bear in mind that objectively speaking, at this moment, since I have never really had any time for pure preparation, I am not now working three days a week. I have to work five or six days a week practically because I have to see witnesses I didn't have the opportunity to see before, and before, to be honest, I met as many witnesses as I could. Sometimes I met with two or three witnesses a day. And the opposing party, as you know, sometimes had five or ten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is very relevant to one of the comments that I made. I have heard what you said, but in assessing it, I cannot ignore the fact that you have available to you assigned counsel, and you are not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. making use of the assigned counsel. You have your associates as well. So you cannot be heard to plead lack of time for preparation when you're not making use of a facility that is available to you. The Appeals Chamber has ruled on this matter. So you cannot -- that will not avail you. It will not avail you with this Trial Chamber to make that argument, and I will totally ignore that argument in assessing questions of time in relation to you. If you make use of assigned counsel --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- and you run into a difficulty with time, that's a different matter. But when you do not make use of assigned counsel, you cannot be heard to say -- you cannot be heard to complain about lack of time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, my associates prepare for me a great deal of documentation and perform a lot of preliminary interviews on my behalf, but you will not contest that I need to see witnesses personally as well. I need to speak to them. So the two working days that are left for me after trial are enough to see two witnesses. I cannot interview 20. You must bear in mind the physical constraints I work under. But let me continue. What you just said, the calculations you made, the arithmetic and the sums you made only show how unrealistic the assigned time is. That's one point. The second point is let us assume that these sums are correct. Based on the practice of Mr. Nice, who made maximum use of Rules 92 bis and 89(F) to introduce a huge amount of material with minimum preliminary examination, it was done to the detriment of the public. I wish to present witnesses here to be heard by the public. I don't wish to unload a truckful of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... detriment of the public because the Trial Chamber ruled that it was permissible, it was evidence that could be given in that way, and naturally the Trial Chamber would have taken into consideration the right of the public to hear the evidence. But I observe that you have selectively, in your recent comments, ignored what I have had to say about assigned counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you mean, Mr. Robinson? In which way did I do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have not mentioned utilising the services of assigned counsel. You have only mentioned your associates. Assigned counsel can help in the preparation of witnesses. That's one of the matters that the Appeals Chamber specifically mentioned. And there are many other ways in which assigned counsel can assist you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, the assigned counsel that you imposed on me represent you, not me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I will not hear that. I will not hear that. That is an absolutely unacceptable comment, to say that the assigned counsel represent me and represent the Chamber. It is a statement which is totally out of order and cannot be substantiated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May I just affirm Your Honour's comments there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But as well, under the order of the Trial Chamber, it's important to bear in mind the accused had an opportunity to appoint his own lawyer to represent him. It doesn't begin and end at Ms. Higgins and myself. He can have as many lawyers here as he likes, I presume, if they were engaged in the case. It doesn't begin and end in me at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's perfectly true. Mr. Milosevic, you have heard what I have had to say on behalf of the Trial Chamber. I want you to bear it in mind. Do not expect any lenience, any accommodation on account of matters relating to time when you do not utilise the services which are available to you. And I'm warning you of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, can you tell me really that somebody, even if they are helping me, can double or triple the time spent here? We spend a certain amount of time here. One day is still one day. I examine witnesses who could, assuming they are helping me, do other jobs at the time; examine witnesses, prepare interviews, et cetera. You are not saying that I'm asking irrelevant questions here or that I'm wasting time. The witnesses who appear here -- who have appeared here so far, answered questions which are important for coming to the truth of the matter, and it will remain so in the future. And it is certainly in my interest --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we have discussed this matter sufficiently. You have heard what I have had to say. Call your next witness now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I call witness Vukasin Andric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please begin, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Dr. Andric.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In order to make rational use of time, I shall say a few things about you at the beginning and you will only answer yes or no. You were born in Kosovo and Metohija; correct?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the village of Raka Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You are a medical doctor, professor at the school of medicine at the university?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You did your entire schooling in Kosovo except for university studies in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, where were you employed? What is your career record? As far as I can see here, you came, after your schooling and specialisation, back to Kosovo and Metohija to work as a doctor.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: In October 1973, I started working in the institute of labour medicine in Pristina, in the electrical company of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So all the time after completing your university studies you worked there until to date?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: With a brief -- with the exception of a brief period in 1978, I worked all the time in Kosovo and Metohija. Correction, 1988.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You became professor at the medical faculty in Kosovo in 1981.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. I passed all the steps from assistant professor to full-time professor, and I am still a full-time professor at the medical faculty of the university in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Throughout this time, you served as the secretary for health in Kosovo and Metohija on the government?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We will now move to the subject matter of your testimony. Tell me, what is the national -- what was the national composition of the employees in health institutions in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija before the NATO aggression?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: In the health institutions of Kosovo and Metohija, many doctors and health workers were employed who were non-Serbs; Albanians, Montenegrins, Muslims, Turks, the Roma, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andric, would you please open tab 1.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gentlemen, I hope you have this entire documentation that has been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the document under tab 1, we see a diagram of the ethnic composition of the employees in public health facilities in the area of the Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija as of 31st December, 1998. Dr. Andric, did you provide this data?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. This data was collected by my services who were employed in the provincial secretariat for health.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this is the data collected by the provincial secretariat for health pertaining to December 1998, the end of the year. Therefore, as we see if we look at the total figures in the last column -- will you please read out the last column.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: 12.599 is the total number of employees in health services. Not only strictly specialised health workers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Serbs, 5.591; 5.301 Albanians; 455 Montenegrins; 420 Muslims; 196 Turks; 69 Gorani, 360 Romas, and 18 declared as Yugoslavs, 14 foreign nationals; 219 others. Now, would you be so kind as to tell me, Dr. Andric, in paragraph 87 of the Kosovo indictment, it says: "After Kosovo's autonomy was effectively revoked in 1989, the political situation in Kosovo became more and more divisive. Throughout late 1990 and 1991, thousands of Kosovo Albanian doctors, teachers, professors --" but I underline doctors, teachers, professors, workers, et cetera -- "were dismissed from their positions." You as someone who worked in Kosovo and Metohija at the time, can you confirm that Kosovo's autonomy was revoked?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did you see it, that time of constitutional changes? How did you live through that as a practising doctor, this period that witnessed the revocation of Kosovo's autonomy? How did you see it as a citizen and a doctor?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Kosovo's autonomy was never revoked. The amendments that were introduced then only confirmed its autonomy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I don't appreciate this desultory manner of leading the witness. I thought you're asking him about the statistics in relation to the doctors in health services, and you referred to paragraph 87, and then you just jumped from that to deal with the question of the revocation of Kosovo's autonomy. Are you finished with the questioning on tab 1?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the document under tab 1, as you can see for yourself, Mr. Robinson, the figures speak for themselves. On the last day of December 1998, 5.301 Albanians were still working, whereas in paragraph 87, the claim is that doctors and health workers were dismissed from their positions. That means nine years before. So those who are claimed to have been dismissed nine years before are still working, 5.301 of them. This is material evidence, real figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It was not clear to me that you had concluded your examination on that issue. Now that you have made it clear, please Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Could tab 1 be an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D280. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andric, in the middle of this paragraph that I read out to you, which you don't have in front of you but it doesn't matter, it says: "Throughout late 1990 and 1991, thousands of Kosovo Albanian doctors and other citizens --" I'm going to ask you only about doctors because you had contacts mostly in that area -- "were dismissed from their positions." Are you aware, at least concerning health institutions and the university, are you aware that there were any dismissals of Albanians? Are you aware that Albanians as such were dismissed, or doctors as such were dismissed from the circles that you moved in?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: The only dismissals were in the cases of serious violations of the legislation in force, specifically the law on labour and labour relations. The greatest number of people consciously and deliberately violated the law in order to be dismissed, but this law was not applied only to Albanians. Anyone who was guilty of an infraction against this law was dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us demystify this law. What does it mean "violation of the law"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, do you have figures for 1989 that we could compare these with, a simple factual matter to see how many people left their employment? In other words, did the secretariat do the same exercise in 1989?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't have that sort of data. I have figures for 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Andric, in 1989, you were serving as a doctor.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You did not have any position in the administration. You were working as a doctor, treating citizens.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Never mind. We'll come back later to that set of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have I wrongly noted that you were actually a professor by 1989, in the same position as you're in at the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1989, I had a position at the medical faculty. I was a young -- I was junior assistant professor. I had just become a lecturer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were talking about dismissals. Could you describe a case in which either an Albanian or a Serb would be dismissed for violating the law.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: There were various cases: If you failed to appear to show up to work for a month, if you refused repeatedly to perform your duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In other words, those are the cases envisaged by the law on labour and labour relations. If somebody doesn't show up for work for a long period of time, then he or she is dismissed.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you say that that was a practice and the legislation that was in force throughout Serbia, not only in Kosovo? For instance, the law said that if you didn't show up for work for five days running without producing a medical certificate, that constitutes grounds for dismissal.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. That law was in force and applied to the entire Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To be more precise, and this will partially respond to Mr. Bonomy's question, did some of them leave their jobs on their own accord?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were a number of such cases of people leaving their jobs voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the reason for them to leave their jobs voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: A large number of them were already deeply involved in the separatist movement. These were people who were very well situated financially. They were very well off. They left their jobs, passed over into parallel institutions, and opened their private practices. I'm speaking of doctors now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to this later. The Albanians who were employed in the health --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. Professor, can I ask you this: If the wording of this paragraph that was quoted to you was different and was in the following terms: "Throughout late 1990 and 1991, thousands of Kosovo Albanian doctors, teachers, professors, workers, police, and civil servants left their positions," would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A large number of them at that time, for various reasons, left their jobs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's time for the break. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, a number of people left their jobs of their own accord. Why?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: In this way, they were defying the legal system of Serbia and at the same time establishing parallel institutions. In this case I'm referring to doctors and professors at the school of medicine. They established their own parallel school of medicine. The doctors who were well off financially, who were affluent, they opened their private practices and worked in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did those Albanians who were employed in the health service and at the university and who did not wish to leave their jobs continue working normally?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. They continued working normally, and they had no problems with the authorities whatsoever. Their only problem were their co-nationals, the separatists who forced them to pay. Every month from their personal funds, they had to pay a certain percentage. This was racketeering. And they were put under constant pressure to leave the state institutions and pass over to the parallel institutions. In this way, both they and members of their families were mistreated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What percentage, Professor, of Albanians left their jobs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can say -- I don't have the precise data, but, Mr. Robinson, I can only say that at the school of law, approximately less than half of the Albanian professors and assistant professors left the faculty of medicine, and the same goes for doctors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The situation you mentioned, that those who remained were put under pressure and maltreated, both they and their family members, did this continue until the beginning of the bombing or did it stop earlier?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: It went on until the bombing began, and it even became more intense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what was the ratio of employed Albanians and Serbs in the health institutions in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: The ratio was 1 to 1, but with reference to doctors on the entire territory of Kosovo and Metohija, this was somewhat in favour of the Albanians. There were somewhat more Albanians than Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please look at tab 2. This is the table showing the number of national structure of employed health workers according to the situation on the day of the 24th of March, 1992, in Kosovo and Metohija. So this is the 24th of March, 1992, the time when the bombing began. 1999, correction. That's in tab 2. This shows doctors, dentists, pharmacists, and other health workers. I assume that "other health workers" refers to nurses and other health professionals.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Unlike the first table which shows only people employed in the health sector -- or, rather, this shows only health professionals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the others are auxiliary staff, such as cleaners, drivers, handymen, and so-and-so forth.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. They're not shown in this table.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this refers only to health professionals. As we can see, 2.087 medical doctors were employed. Of these, 1.008 were Albanians, 847 were Serbs, 66 were Montenegrins, 20 were Turks, and 146 were others. Who were the others?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: All those who lived on the territory of Serbia. Serbia is a multi-ethnic state, and the others include Macedonians, Greeks, Bulgarians, Romanians, Ruthenians, Croats, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says here that on the 24th of March, 1999, the number of employed health workers in all health institutions. There were 4.462 Albanians, and this is 47 per cent, while there were 5 -- 4.248 or, rather, 5.002 others who were not Albanians, Serbs and others. Does that include all the others?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In tab 2 we also have the number and ethnic composition of employees in the health institutions who were health professionals on the 24th of March, 1999, by health institution: Pristina, Istok, Pec, Djakovica, Prizren, Dragas, Zvecan, Mitrovica, Gnjilane, Vitina. Is there something to which you would like to draw attention?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. There are several things I would like to point out. Depending on the concentration of certain ethnic groups, the percentage of employees changed. So that in Djakovica, for example, there are 605 Albanians and 70 Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me correct you. 70 Serbs and Montenegrins.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And 605 Albanians.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Whereas in Pristina the ratio was somewhat more favourable. In Prizren, for example, there were more Albanians again, in Kosovska Mitrovica slightly more Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "Pristina," under number 4 it says University Health Centre of Pristina. The situation favours the Serbs at the university centre?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does this have any connection with the level of education among the Serbian and Albanian population?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, because you could never see this ratio among the employed Serbs and Albanians in health institutions in comparison with other institutions such as railway, farms, and so on because there were more Serbs who were highly educated and who got jobs in the -- at the university.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, there must be some difference between these two tables on tab 2. The total number in the first one is 9.570.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The total in the second one is 13.134. Can you say Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. why there is the difference in the total? Does the second one take account of more than simply health professionals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, precisely so. The second table includes other workers as well, Mr. Bonomy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. In the second table, you have practically two tables, one up to the 24th of March, 1999, and the second from the 10th of September, 1999. This table shows that in most of these centres except for Dragas, Zvecan and Kosovska Mitrovica there were no Serbs left at all.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, this is the situation at present, I can say, in Kosovo and Metohija. Health workers were mostly expelled from Kosovo and Metohija except for Serbs in Kosovska Mitrovica and that only in the northern part of Kosovska Mitrovica. The other Serb professionals were expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, all the professors and assistant lecturers at Pristina University who were of Albanian ethnicity, did they leave their jobs in the clinics and institutes?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: No. A large of professors and assistant lecturers of Albanian ethnicity remained and worked in the clinical hospital centre and the institutions of the school of medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you give us an example according to the best of your recollection of prominent Albanians who remained working at the university? I wish to draw your attention to tab 3 where you drew up a list of those who remained at posts in the Pristina city hospital after 1999.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have the list here, and there is a mistake here. It says 1999. It should read 1991. This is a typographical error.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: I remember very well Professor Dzevat Nurboja who remained and who taught at the Serbian school of medicine. And the same status was held by Dr. Tefik Ljeci, an assistant professor from forensic medicine. And I can enumerate many other eminent Albanian professors who remained after 1991 and worked in the medical institutes and clinics, including Professor Esref Bicaku, Professor Dzemal Bajraktari, Professor Hisri Tafarshiku, Professor Bedri Bakali, Professor Hamid Ramsi [phoen], Professor Meshqyre Capuni-Brestovci, Professor Muharem Kutlovci, Professor Muharem Bajrami, and many others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In tab 3 you have a list of professors and lecturers who remained at the university after 1991. You have them listed by section; ophthalmology, surgery, neuropsychiatry, infective diseases, pulmology, internal medicine, anatomy, patophysiology, physiology, pharmacology, pathological anatomy, biochemistry, forensic medicine, stomatology, radiology, and so on. According to your knowledge, there's also paediatrics. So they all remained at their jobs, those are the ones listed in tab 3?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, going back slightly to the earlier tab, in the second part of the second table, that's from the 10th of September, 1999, where would you appear on that table?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where would I appear on this table?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Should you not be there somewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should not be here on this table from the 10th of September. I should be but, unfortunately, I'm not. I should be in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought you were still working in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, no. I left Pristina on the 25th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't understand this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Tab 2 as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This table to which Mr. Bonomy drew attention shows that in primary health care in Pristina, there is not a single Serb. In health protection in Pristina there is no Serb. Transfusology in Pristina, no Serb. University Health Centre in Pristina, not a single Serb. Pharmaceutical institutions in Pristina, not a single Serb. In Istok, again, not a single Serb. In Pec, not a single Serb. In Djakovica, not a single Serb. In the health centre in Pec and the special hospital in Pec and all these institutions, Prizren, Dragas -- in Dragas there are two, in Zvecan there are 8, and in Kosovska Mitrovica 703 health professionals. Of all the centres, there are only two Serbs and Montenegrins in Dragas, eight in Zvecan, and 703 in Kosovska Mitrovica. That's all, as far as I can see from this table. Is this information correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps now there are a few more in Mitrovica because in the meantime something has changed, but for the most part this is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. These professors listed in tab 3 who continued working after 1991, you mentioned that some of them lectured in the Serbian language and continued working as health professionals. Did they have any difficulties as far as the way they were treated by the administration, the management, the institutions they worked in, or the authorities?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: No. They had no problems whatsoever. They had exactly same rights and obligations as all the other employees in those institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Professor, these departments, who headed them? Take, for example, ophthalmology. Who would have been the head of ophthalmology; a Serb or an Albanian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These two departments were headed by Serbs, but I will mention, for example, biochemistry where there was an Albanian professor, Burhan Dida, who was even in the management of all the institutes.
