utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And generally, though, who were the heads of these departments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were more Serbs who were heads of departments than others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, please tell me about what you know. What guided those who left their positions, and what was the reason for some Albanian professors and professionals to remain working? I would like to hear both sides as you know it. Therefore, what guided those who left their jobs, and what guided those who remained?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Those who left their jobs were members of separatist movement --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... going to be asked this sort of question. I'm not sure that we shouldn't first hear what is the root to his being able to provide any kind of answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He might have heard from them. He can state it as a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He might have done, but in my submission we should hear about this first. And also I must draw to the Chamber's attention that we have to work on 65 ter summaries. A 65 ter summary makes -- makes no specific reference to the medical background. It makes the most passing reference to the background. Now, if I'm supposed to deal with these witnesses as I wish to do, efficiently and in a compact way, without a 65 ter summary of the detail -- giving detail of what the evidence is going to be, it's very hard for us. On this particular matter, if we're going to have a summary of the reasons for witnesses -- not witnesses, other people doing one thing or another, it's probably going to be impossible for me to deal with it in cross-examination and I shall have to make that position clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, in relation to this question, you must ascertain from the witness the source of the information as to why they left. If he knows, then how did he acquire that information?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have mentioned very briefly that they were linked to the separatist movement. How do you know about their links with the separatist movement, those people who left their jobs?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: That was obvious based on everyday contacts. In addition, they left their jobs, went to the illegal school of medicine. Most of them or, rather, all of them who left their jobs went to the illegal medical school, and in addition to that, opened private practices or private clinics where they worked. These private practices and clinics could only have been opened based on a prior approval of state authorities which they obtained from the Ministry of Health. Based on that, they opened their private medical practices and earned ten times what they would have earned at state agencies. And by doing so, they benefited twice because on one hand they portrayed themselves as persecuted people, people who were persecuted by Serbia, which was not true, and on the other hand, they increased tenfold their income and didn't have to pay taxes on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So in order for them to obtain licenses and permits for opening private practices, the procedure for that was the same everywhere in Serbia, where the Ministry of Health had to evaluate whether they were qualified, whether they fulfilled all requirements in order to open private practices. Was there a political criterion there or just a professional one?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: There was no political criterion there. The Ministry of Health or its subordinate offices issued those permits. And I have to tell you that in view of the number of such private practices, the large majority of them were owned by Albanians. Very few were owned by Serbs, and all the rest were Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We have tab 4 here, and you've provided here a list of professors and assistant professors of the medical school in Pristina of Albanian origin who, after leaving their jobs, opened their own private practices and clinics. We can see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are these the ones earning tenfold what they would have earned working for the government, Professor? According to your earlier evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, sir, yes. They earned ten times what they would have earned in the public health system of Serbia. However, that was privilege available only to those who were affluent, who had enough money to open their private practices. For me, that was something that was not available to me. I could only have dreamed about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You just used the colloquialism, what we're trying to say, actually.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: I was trying to say that that option was impossible for me, was not available for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Andric, in paragraph 88 of the Kosovo indictment, it says: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. "During this period, the unofficial Kosovo Albanian leadership pursued a policy of non-violent civil resistance and began establishing a system of unofficial, parallel institutions in the health care and education sectors." My question is: This phenomenon of people leaving jobs voluntarily that you just described, was that an integral part of, as is stated here, this non-violent resistance?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: No. This deliberate voluntary leaving of jobs was aimed at creating parallel institutions. They left their jobs and established parallel institutions. The creation of parallel institutions in health care and education sectors is a mechanism through which they pursued this non-violent resistance, although I don't understand how can a resistance be non-violent? In my view, every resistance has to be violent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is an academic issue now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the indictment doesn't allege that the leaving of the jobs was what constituted this non-violent civil resistance. So I don't know. You may be answering an allegation that is not there. But continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Tab 3 to be an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I don't know if I quoted this correctly, but it says here "... the unofficial Kosovo Albanian leadership during this period pursued a policy of non-violent civil resistance and began establishing a system of non-parallel institutions in the health care and education sectors." I quoted this accurately from paragraph 88. So my question was whether this deliberate leaving of jobs was an integral part of this allegedly non-violent resistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He has answered it, so we can move on. He has already answered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have also mentioned that there in fact was violence there, too. Was there violence against Albanian teachers and assistant professors which was used in order to force them to leave their jobs or not, based on what you know?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: I already answered that question partially. All of those who remained were subjected to various forms of pressure. They had to pay a portion of their salary, and this was mandatory. This was done every month. I witnessed this myself. And they were also subjected to various forms of pressure which was aimed at making them leave their jobs and transferring to parallel institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Those who already transferred to parallel institutions, did they do that voluntarily or under pressure?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Some of them transferred voluntarily. However, most of them had to transfer under pressure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Nice will no doubt about asking about this, but I might as well ask: To whom was it mandated that a portion of the salary had to be paid? You have made this allegation, but you haven't given any details. So I'm asking you. First, who subjected those who remained to various forms of pressure; and secondly, to whom was a portion of the salary paid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Robinson, it was paid to the leadership of the separatist movement, the separatist movement of Albanians. This movement for many years, for decades, was active not only in Kosovo and Metohija but also throughout other countries as well. They collected contributions in order to develop the separatist movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How did you acquire this information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my clinic, every month when the salaries were paid out, a man would come, a man whom I didn't know, who made lists and collected money from the employees of my clinic, which was ears, nose and throat clinic. This was a rule that applied to all employees in the entire territory of Kosovo and Metohija and also to private entrepreneurs and everybody who had an income.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Their departure from their jobs, you explained to us that they left under pressure exerted by the separatist movement. Did you see anybody leave their jobs under the pressure of authorities?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: I have no such information. I didn't see any of such cases nor do I know of any such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The leaving of jobs and everything else you describe, did it create a picture, an impression that the human rights of Albanians were violated or denied to them?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Certainly. It was certainly that way, because this entire organisation was aimed at that, to portray themselves as victims and to show to the international public this alleged persecution of Albanians in order to use it for their goals later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I've mentioned to you this when I quoted the paragraph where doctors, teachers are mentioned, and so on. Therefore, parallel institutions were established both in the health care and education sectors. Do you know something about the creation of parallel institutions in the education sector as well?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. The parallel institutions in education were established much more thoroughly and diligently than the ones in the health care sector. The reason for that is very simple; because of the numbers. There were many more people, and the youth had to be indoctrinated for the goals of the separatist movement. In addition to that, the parallel institutions in education sidestepped the Republic of Serbia and its curricula. They introduced the curriculum of the Republic of Albania. And by establishing parallel institutions in education, they showed just what was the extent of their resistance in relation to the official system of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In the education sector, where did they -- what did they emphasise especially?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: They particularly emphasised geography, literature, and history.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why history?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Because by falsifying history, they wanted to show that they were in -- their ancestors were actually the Illyrians and that they were the oldest people inhabiting that area and that all other nations who arrived later had no right to Kosovo, no claim to the Kosovo land.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about geography?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Geography for the simple reason that they wanted to abolish the use of Serbian and Slav place names, and by doing so they wanted to show that they were the oldest people who arrived to Kosovo and that everybody else came later. The place names were especially named -- especially changed after the Second World War, and after the arrival of the UN forces to Kosovo and Metohija practically all Serb or Slav place names were abolished. Let me give you just several examples. Srbica became Skenderaj; Glogova became Kastriot; Leposavac, where no Albanians lived ever, became Albanac; Vucitrn became Vushtrri, and so on. So not a single place name of Slav origin exists in Kosovo and Metohija. They have all been changed, then substituted with Albanian place names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about literature?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The transcript says especially changed after the Second World War and after the arrival of the UN forces in Kosovo and Metohija all Serb or Slav place names were abolished. Was the change made after the Second World War or after the arrival of the UN forces or both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for putting that question, Mr. Robinson. After the Second World War there was a attempt to change place names and they did manage to change certain place names. They started from a thesis which was pursued by Enver Hodzic during his brief rule in Albania. He changed, especially in northern Albania, all Serbian place names. And there were many of them, there was a majority of them there. So he replaced them with Albanian place names and he -- he converted Christians, Orthodox Christians, to Catholics and to Muslims. There were attempts for many years to pursue the same policy in Kosovo and Metohija after the Second World War. I can quote several examples to you. Djeneral Jankovic was called Hani i Elezit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now, what happened after the arrival of the UN forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the arrival of the UN forces, all Serb and Slav place names were completely abolished in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. These place names simply do not exist any more. Let me tell you, larger towns, such as Srbica, have been renamed. Srbica became Skenderaj. Glogovac became Kastriot; Leposavac became Albanac; Vucitrn became Vushtrri, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned literature. What can you tell us about the way that literature was taught? What was their emphasis there?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Through glorifying their historical heroes in their literature, they created -- they turned them into historical myths, and they used those myths to educates their youth and to instill national and separatist sentiments in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You told us that the parallel institutions in the education sector were more successful than parallel institutions in the health care sector, which is understandable to me because in the health care sector you need professionals, experts. Therefore, tell me, please, in relation to that, what was the percentage of patients therefore - not the staff but, rather, the patients - in the health services with regard to their ethnic background, patients seeking medical assistance and treatment?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Throughout my career and throughout my life, I lived in Kosovo and Metohija, and that percentage of patients was always 19 -- 90 per cent of Albanians, 10 per cent of others. And that remained unchanged even after the establishment of the so-called parallel institutions in health care.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So 90 per cent of those who needed health care were Albanians?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. And even if they had attempted to receive appropriate medical assistance in parallel health care institutions, they failed and had to go to public health care institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have to remind you to speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: So 90 per cent of our patients were Albanians. Some of them had gone to private clinics and other private institutions but could not resolve their problems there and had to turn to public health care centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to see any case of discrimination or unfair treatment on the part of health care staff in Kosovo and Metohija vis-a-vis the Albanian patients who, as you said, made up 90 per cent of the total?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: No. The Hippocratic Oath was strictly observed. I can say that in my long career, I was always deliberately more careful with Albanians than with Serbs precisely in order to avoid an error that could be misconstrued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, about these parallel institutions that you talked about in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the education sector, in health care, what was the attitude of the authorities towards them? I mean state authorities, to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: The attitude of the state authorities was decent, correct. They kept trying, through legislation, to embrace them in the system of the state institutions to cover them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there an agreement, an attempt to normalise the situation, an agreement signed even by Rugova?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were several attempts to normalise the situation. I think the most noteworthy one was in 1996 when a mixed Albanian-Serb commission was formed under the aegis of a Vatican led by Monsignor Doctor Vincenzo Paglia. The name of the organisation was Sant'Egidio. Measures were developed to normalise the situation, especially in university institutions. However, this remained fruitless because the Albanian side didn't do anything to actually implement it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that the state authorities put everything in place, made available buildings and facilities and everything that was necessary to implement this agreement?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that. The Albanian side was given the building of the engineering faculty, among others, the most beautiful building that we have, the building of the law school, the building of the faculty of arts, the teachers training college. All this -- all these facilities were handed over to the Albanian side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm sorry to interrupt you on a procedural matter, but in relation to the remarks that I made on behalf of the Chamber about time, let us try to begin with this witness whom you had scheduled for six hours. I'd like you to try to complete the examination-in-chief within four hours. We can work until 2.00 today, and then you will try to finish by the end of the first session tomorrow, and the Prosecutor would also be kept within limits. But I am not placing a time limit on you because it was not the practice to place a time limit on examination-in-chief for the Prosecutor. But I'm really trying to assist you to use your time in the best way possible. So let us try and conclude this witness within four hours, and we work until 2.00 and -- well, I'm just understanding we can't work until 2.00 because one of our members has another judicial engagement but -- yes, we'll work until 2.00, and I'm encouraging you -- exhorting you to try to complete this witness by the end of the first session tomorrow, which would be four hours and 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can tab 4 be an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do my best, Mr. Robinson. It is in my interest to use as little time as possible, because I want to bring as many witnesses as I can. It is definitely not in my interest to prolong the examination of any witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To be as clear as possible, Mr. Andric, we have already mentioned these attempts by Albanian separatists, the constant efforts to attract the sympathies of the international public. I want to ask you about one scandal about a case and what you know about it. In spring 1993, certain media, including international media, were flooded by news about alleged poisoning of students and pupils and children by some gas. This notorious scandal about the poisoning of children with gas that was topical in spring 1990.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. I worked as a doctor, and I witnessed all this. In spring 1990, more precisely beginning with March and ending with June that year, the entire territory of Kosovo and Metohija was flooded by some alleged poisoning of Albanian children and students. The allegation was that the authorities were behind this. I will explain what was going on, because I was in Pristina. In most places around Pristina at the same time, about ten cars would set out driving the so-called victims of poisoning, and with the screeching of tyres and a lot of noise, they would stop in front of the Pristina clinical centre where medical teams would be waiting with stretchers. They would bring these so-called victims every day so that there would be hundreds of admissions per day in the health centres. And even serious patients were discharged in order to make room for these newly arrived. Ludicrous situations were occurring. Blood drips and IV drips were placed in the pillow instead of the vein, and other ludicrous things were happening. There were television crews and cameras present whose task was to show to the world this alleged suffering of the Albanian people in Kosovo. This was common throughout Kosovo and Metohija, but Pristina was the hardest hit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have some footage to show, and I will ask the AV booth to run it. It's under tab 5. This is just one clip that I would like to introduce through this witness, but I would like to point out this is only a brief segment of what was recorded, because a lot of this was happening during the war, and there was very little possibility to make recordings. You have all been supplied with a translation of these video clips?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tab 5, transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 5. And then clip by clip, you will find the translations of what is being said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we have 18 segments in total.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All this is under tab 5, but we will go through them one by one, because this one refers to the poisoning scandal, and the others refer to the period of the war in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "It's a shame, because the Oscars are being handed out tomorrow. "Gashi says today that we see polymorphous symptoms today, a term that he himself is unable to translate adequately or be more specific, but I quote the therapy is well chosen. What remains unclear is what is a well-chosen therapy for a disease that remains unknown. "A reporter asks: Which therapy? "Aljusi Gashi replies: The right therapy is the one that helps remove those symptoms, but I don't have it here. "[No interpretation]"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We didn't get any --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We didn't have any translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry if you didn't get the translation. I thought it was under this tab. The written translation is provided under this tab, and you heard that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a translation into English of what these doctors were saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us not waste time. I want to ask the witness for a comment. We saw in the beginning the patients running towards their beds. What was that all about?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: It speaks of the gravity of poisoning. Those were young people who were completely healthy, who were brought to hospital to be portrayed as sick, and then they would walk along the corridors of the hospital, and then when a TV crew or somebody would arrive, they would run to their beds and make believe that they were poisoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We saw them being urgently transported to the hospital en masse. Where were they allegedly poisoned? What were the allegations?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: The allegation was that they were poisoned throughout schools in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Kosovo schools where there were only Serbs -- where there were Serbs and Albanians or only Albanians?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: There were both Albanian and Serb children there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How come, then, that only Albanians were poisoned in the same building?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Of course it was not possible, but it was necessary to demonise Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I ask, when they were brought to the hospital, all these thespians, these actors, were they examined by the doctors to determine whether they were in fact poisoned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour, Mr. Robinson. We examined them, we did laboratory and toxicological tests, we examined seriously every young man and woman until we had definitively proven that they were not ill. Even if they were not medically ill, we treated them as ill because they had agreed to be manipulated in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what did the tests show? Did you do the urine and blood tests?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did everything to establish if there was any poisoning or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In any of these hundreds of cases, was there any real poisoning established?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: The numbers were not in the hundreds but in the thousands. Not in a single case was it proven that there was any poisoning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in that entire scandal, did anybody die?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: No. No one was even poisoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody develop a disorder or disease that could later be treated?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So how did the medical staff in Kosovo and Metohija treat this monoethnic poisoning?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: I will have to speak about the Serb and Albanian medical staff separately. Serb --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does it matter for this case how they were treated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it is important, Your Honour, Judge Bonomy. At least, you will see if you hear my answer. Serbs did their job professionally. As for the Albanian medical staff, I could divide them into three groups. The first group were organisers. There were few of them. The second, largest group were all of those who had agreed consciously to participate in this whole farce, trampling on their Hippocratic Oath and their professional duty, and the third group were those who offered passive or active resistance, but there were few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Although there were few of them, as you say, do you know of any Albanian doctors or medical staff who resisted this farce, who tried to do something? Can you give us their names?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: I know two Albanian professors. I don't know if it's a good idea to mention them here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We can go into private session for just two minutes, if you wanted to give us their names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why do you need their names?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that their names can be heard Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. here and entered into the record to show that there were Albanian professors who condemned this whole scandal about the alleged poisoning in which no one died, no one fell ill, and all the laboratory tests failed to confirm a single claim of poisoning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... allegation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevance is that there was constant talk of some sort of maltreatment of Albanians, about evil done by Serbs to Albanians, about the demonisation of Serbs in this manner, which was simply pure theatre and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll have the names, then, in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Andric, as this was a major scandal and was widely reported, both abroad and in our country, let me ask you specifically, did the federal institutions and the institutions of the Republic of Serbia take any action in connection with this scandal?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Very soon after the first cases of alleged poisoning were reported, a helicopter arrived from Belgrade, bringing a delegation including the director of the federal institution of health protection, Dr. Branko Dragas, and on behalf of the Ministry of Health of the Republic of Serbia, Professor Bozo Antonijevic, an expert on toxicology. They examined the case, saw what this was about, went back to Belgrade. They, of course, established that there was no poisoning, but in order to lend credence to all this, the Federal Secretariat for Health established an 11-member commission, including experts from clinical hospital centres in Ljubljana, Zagreb and Belgrade, and this commission submitted its report in early June to the health committee of the Federal Assembly. This report said that there was no poisoning and that not a single case of poisoning had been established.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We have here in tab 6 a report, a newspaper report about the discussion conducted by the Executive Council Committee for Labour, Health, and Welfare. The title is "There was no poisoning." The Committee of the Executive Council --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to intervene, loath though I am to do it. This whole issue was originally raised by the accused in cross-examination of a witness, and I think I asked one question of a later witness about the same topic and I can't remember how it arose. It seems to me that it is inconceivable that this Trial Chamber will be able to make a final decision about whether thousands and thousands of people were masquerading as ill, and pretty unlikely if not inconceivable that the Trial Chamber will regard it as sufficiently relevant to form an important part of its judgement, or any part of its judgement. Now, this report - I don't mind the Chamber reading it - but I wonder really how this report is really going to add to the material that the Chamber has to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: First of all, if I might speak on this, it would be helpful to have the official report, but I think more directly, Mr. Nice, if you make the allegations or the averments you make in paragraphs 87 and 88 of the Kosovo indictment, is it not inevitable that we will end up examining issues such as this? Which you may be right but if you are right it begs the question why they're in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They were in the indictment as background matters and it's a matter for the Chamber the degree to which it's proper to go into them in detail. They're there. I haven't objected. I don't necessarily object now, but I do raise as an issue, given the Chamber's earlier observations about the best use of time, whether this report, which is obviously being adduced in whatever format for the truth of its content, is going to be a material bit of evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic evidently attaches great forensic value to background matters. But, Mr. Milosevic, this is a background matter, and you may not want to spend so much time on it. You have been dealing with this now for about half an hour, this single issue of the poisoning. I think you should move on to another -- move on to another matter. It has been sufficiently ventilated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can tab 5.1 be an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have completed this topic in a shorter time than it took to make this objection, because from this large article talking about the work of the federal, not the republican but the federal, institutions I just wanted to quote what Dr. Branko Pocek said. You can tell by his name that he's evidently not a Serb. And on the occasions of the findings of the commission, he said that "Ethical norms of the Hippocratic Oath have been trampled on in Kosovo because health workers have put themselves in the service of certain political goals." It was clear, therefore, that this was a scam, that this was put up and the fact that several thousand people took part in it, in this stage-managed farce --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm stopping you and I'm requiring you to move on to another topic. The indictment will not stand or fall on the basis of this single allegation. Next topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson. Mr. Nice speaks of the general context, and it is only based on the background.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just tell me this, please: Do you remember from this period of time that these official findings of experts - federal, republican and other experts on Kosovo and Metohija - were publicised in the foreign media in any way or were given nearly as much publicity as the story on the alleged poisonings? Do you remember that time?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, the official findings were never given any significance in the media. This was never refuted in the media. Unfortunately, it was the first story about the poisoning that was left to stand and it was not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall any other examples of this kind of mass abuse for propaganda purposes from, for example, 1998, 1999?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's -- I'm not allowing that. I'm not allowing that question. It has a leading element in it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Without any leading elements in my question, do you remember an event, let's just mention it very briefly and please make your answer brief, from 1989 concerning the so-called miner's strike in Stari Trg?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was in February 1989, from the 28th of February. 1.300 Albanian miners went on strike. They remained in the pit and their demands were purely political. They wanted the replacement of three Albanian leaders, the federal, provincial, and city leaders who were pro-Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that in October 1998 you were the secretary for health?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall -- I'm referring to October, 1998 -- do you recall an event in the village of Resnik near Vucitrn where the population was exclusively Albanian? What happened there on the 29th of October, 1998?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: The village of Resnik near Vucitrn is a village populated exclusively by Albanians, and in October on a field near the mosque, suddenly about 25.000 people gathered, mostly women, children, and elderly men. They had been brought in for days from neighbouring areas, mostly from the areas of Vucitrn, Mitrovica, Srbica and Glogova. They were -- Srbica and Glogova. They were brought in by trucks and other vehicles and they asked that the High Commissioner for Refugees, Madam Sadako Ogata, address them personally. They said that the Serbian army and police were expelling them from their homes, persecuting them, and that they were living out in the open. Mrs. Ogata arrived. She addressed them briefly, and this was recorded by all the leading world media, by their cameras, and several minutes after Mrs. Sadako Ogata left the area, they peacefully went back to their homes, leaving behind only plastic bags and other litter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, 25.000 Albanian refugees were shown on the media, and after Mrs. Ogata left, they returned home and weren't there any more, only the following days. Is this what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. And there are many such examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Andric, in what period were you regional secretary for health?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: I was provincial secretary for health of Kosovo and Metohija from early October 1998 until March 2002 when the temporary provincial council stopped its work. It was disbanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: While performing this duty, did you meet people from the Verification Mission? From October 1998 throughout this time, the Verification Mission was present. Did you meet members and leaders of the Verification Mission of the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. During that period, late 1998, 1999, until the 29th of March, 1999, when the Verification Mission left Kosovo and Metohija, I met many members of this OSCE mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And did you have contacts with anyone from the medical sector of that mission, those dealing with health issues?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. After the end of the Rambouillet negotiations and just before the Paris negotiations, I personally received the head of this section. It was the Finnish -- it was a Finnish doctor, I don't recall his name, and we spoke in my office in the provincial council.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what did he want to learn from you? What did he draw your attention to?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: For the most part he wanted me to tell him about the way the health service in Kosovo and Metohija was organised and structured.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you explain this to him?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes, briefly, to the extent he was interested in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that he then, as could be expected, made some comments or objections or gave you some suggestions. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember well that his main objection was that it's too centralised and too connected to Belgrade, that it should be less centralised and less linked to Belgrade. He asked whether we needed any aid from the international community as regards health services.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did he in any way draw attention to any violations of human rights or improper behaviour by the authorities or the health institutions, health organs?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: No. This was a very pleasant spontaneous conversation in which we discussed organisation. There were no objections apart from the one I mentioned. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of the number of humanitarian organisations from abroad on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija in late 1998 and early 1999?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was the provincial secretary for health and this was part of my job. On the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, just before the NATO aggression, there were 29 foreign humanitarian organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what happened? Do you have anything to say about what they were doing, these humanitarian organisations, to what extent they cooperated with the health organs in Kosovo and Metohija of which you were at the head as the provincial secretary for health?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. They had free access to the entire territory of Kosovo and Metohija. They were able to reach every part of the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. They gave quite a lot of assistance to the health institutions on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija in terms of medicines and medical material and equipment, supplies, and they were carrying out their humanitarian mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And what happened to these organisations on the eve of the NATO aggression?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: When Walker's Kosovo Verification Mission left a week before the beginning of the NATO aggression, all these humanitarian organisations left the territory of Kosovo and Metohija; all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they take with them all their property when they were leaving? Did they take all their belongings?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: No. They took some movable belongings but they left warehouses throughout the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what happened to their warehouses? What did you find there?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Well, when the NATO aggression started, unknown perpetrators looted many of these and raided many of these warehouses. However, some of them were left, and we looked at what was inside. There was a warehouse belonging to an organisation called Handicap where, apart from medical supplies and medicines, I found many crutches, wheelchairs and such equipment. This would not have been surprising had these things not been present in impossibly large quantities. This was quite scary. This heralded war, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any contacts with the NGO Medecins sans Frontieres?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was your experience with this organisation?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. They arrived on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija in 1993. They worked without any hindrance or obstruction on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, and they helped quite a lot. I remember, for example, the waterworks in Vucitrn and they brought medicines and other equipment, but I learned from the field at one point that part of this humanitarian organisation, its individual members, were engaging in impermissible actions and that some of them had become the medical corps of the KLA, the so-called KLA. In early 1999, they asked -- they applied to me to extend their permit because they had to extend their permit every three months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are at the time for the break. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Andric, we discussed your contacts with the organisation Medecins sans Frontieres. Please take a look at tab 7. This is dated 4th of January, 1999. This is a statement for the public given by the provincial secretary of health, Dr. Vukasin Andric. In order not to waste time, let us cover this briefly. You gave a statement for the public and it is stated here that the Doctors Without Borders abused their white coats when they accepted to smuggle and hide weapons for Albanian terrorists. This is at the end of the first paragraph of your statement. Not only that, our public and the entire world was informed that one of their teams was uncovered using a frequency solely reserved for communication by members of the Ministry of the Interior. And then it says that the monitors are using a humane and noble idea in order to directly or indirectly assist terrorists and terrorism. And then in the last paragraph, that such a conduct contributes to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation in Kosovo and Metohija. Therefore, you as the health secretary stated this with respect to the conduct of the Doctors Without Borders, and you had information when you made this statement. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The cooperation with Doctors Without Borders, did you discuss it with the chief of their office, Mr. Boucher?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tab 8, does it contain a record from the meeting with Boucher?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is quite long. The Serbian version is. It has three pages. The English translation has two pages but that is irrelevant. I will stick to the Serbian text. You say here that Vukasin Andric explained that he received information about the Doctors Without Borders from several sources, from several people that he contacted in the field. This is in the third paragraph. And they included people from all ethnic groups, mostly from Albanians, or the majority were Albanians. Some sources included journalists and representatives of official organs. And then in the next paragraph it says it doesn't matter how and when somebody was caught with weapons but that the assistance is not provided to both sides, and then you explain that the idea of humanitarian organisation is not to distinguish among the people of different religions or ethnic backgrounds. So you emphasised this. Did you have any reason to believe that they were insisting on assisting only Albanians and not the other side, the non-Albanian population?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes, partially. What I said was that they were helping the health institutions in the area of Kosovo and Metohija. We had no complaints there. However, what was impossible to understand was that a humanitarian organisation which comes to a situation -- to a territory which is multi-ethnic, which contains several ethnic communities, employs, in the course of six years, only members of one ethnic community. This means that Doctors Without Borders, in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, employed solely Albanians regardless of whether they were doctors, nurses, staff, general staff or not. All of them were Albanians, exclusively Albanians. The staff of Doctors Without Borders lived in houses and apartments owned exclusively by Albanians, which you will agree with me caused suspicion among Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 2 in paragraph two from the bottom you say that Dr. Andric explained that this did not have to be a political discussion, only agreements on specific activities, and then Boucher, in the following passage, says that they wanted to cooperate with both sides, they wanted to go to Serbian villages too but encountered animosity. So what was this all about? With did they encounter animosity in Serbian villages?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: I don't think that they encountered animosity in Serbian villages at all. It's simply that the Serbs knew -- you know how it was. When the situation is tense and a doctor comes from Doctors Without Borders and brings with him an Albanian driver, an Albanian nurse, and so on, this automatically creates mistrust. And knowing what was done until then, people simply did not trust that organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the end of this record of yours, you say that one Albanian doctor was killed in Pec in the most awful way because he did not want to accept the invitation extended to him by the terrorists to go and work for Doctors Without Borders. So you claim that he was killed because of that. And then Boucher replies to you, in the penultimate paragraph, that he heard about the case but had no contacts with that person. He said that he had no influence over the media or politics and that's why he wanted to explain what they were really doing and what they should cooperate more closely.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: This involved Dr. Dzevad Gashi, who remained working in the Serbian health care system. That night when he was killed, and he was killed several days before my meeting with Mr. Boucher, which took place on the 22nd of January, 1999 - I remember this well - this doctor went to his work and was killed by the terrorists of the so-called KLA. His parents stated to the television that several days before he was killed, members of the so-called KLA had come and tried to pressure him into leaving his job with the Serb republic institutions and go to work for the Doctors Without Borders.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I ask that this exhibit be tendered into evidence, this record reflecting the conversation he held -- he had with Mr. Boucher. This is tab 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Tab 7 was referred to as well as part of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 7 and 8, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Andric, where were you at the time when the NATO aggression against Yugoslavia started; and did you hold any other positions or offices during the NATO aggression?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: When the NATO aggression against Yugoslavia started, I was in Pristina preparing, together with my team, the work of health services which were supposed to adapt to the -- to the war conditions, and in addition to being the provincial health secretary, I was also president of the staff of humanitarian issues and also member of the civilian protection staff and member of the staff for coordinating between civilian authorities, army, and the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. You mentioned several organs just now. Please tell us something about the composition of these organs. When I say "the composition," what I have in mind is both professional background of its members and ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: The composition was quite diverse. People from various professional backgrounds were involved and also people from various ethnic communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, let us please look at tab 9, which is a decision appointing you. This is a form. The decision appointing you president of the staff on humanitarian issues and assistance to the displaced persons returning to their homes. And then in the statement of reasons, it is stated that the staff has to coordinate the activities pursuant to the plan and programme of work and activities. There is a translation into English. And then it says that they are duty-bound to pay special attention to ensuring that there are favourable conditions for housing civilian population, assisting economic organisations, especially health care organs, to ensure law and order, protect property, prevent any action taken against the liberty of citizens, and then this last bit is covered by the seal, to facilitate the return of displaced persons to their homes. Therefore, what can you tell us about the work of these organs, the work in which you participated? Did your work involve all of these Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. activities described here as the activities undertaken by the staff?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Our duty was to help civilian population, especially those who were at risk, but not only those who were in danger or at risk but everybody who lived in that territory. All of them needed to receive basic necessities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What were your specific tasks? Just give us the main ones. What were your main duties?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: For example, we dealt with ensuring that there was clean water, also protection of environmental area, provision of medical assistance, ensuring that there was food for people who lacked food. We were also involved in removing the consequences of NATO bombing. Where there were dead people or casualties, we ensured that action was taken and then we also undertook sanitisation of the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andric, I made a mistake. I read out the document under tab 10 rather than the document under tab 9. So let us go back to tab 9, which is the decision - please take a look at the document in tab 9 - establishing the staff for humanitarian issues which is going to be composed of the following persons, and then Vukasin Andric is the chairman; Veljko Odalovic, member; Zejnelabidin Kurejs, member; Selim Gudjufi, member; Faik Jashari, member; and then Mihajlo Nedic, member. And then the document goes on to explain the duties of the staff. So please tell us, the members of the staff, what was their ethnicity? There was a total of six of them.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: There were Serbs, Turks, Albanians, and a Montenegrin there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. This is tab 9. I would like this decision, which has a registration number and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- is dated April 1999, as well as tab 10, which I have already covered, be tendered into evidence. Tab 10 pertains --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- to the appointment of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Andric, before the bombing started, did the residents leave Pristina and other cities as well as the territory of Kosovo and Metohija in general?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: No. Before the NATO aggression started, the movement of the population was a regular one. Regular life was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about after the bombing started?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: After the bombing started, the very first day, and the bombing started in the evening of the 24th of March, so already on the next day, on the 25th of March, I noticed groups of people in Pristina leaving the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Who was leaving town? When I say "who," I'm referring to the ethnicity of the people leaving town.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Everybody was leaving town. That means Albanians, Serbs, Roma; everybody living there. The -- the rule that applied was that everybody was leaving town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were in Pristina then.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did the number of people leaving Pristina increase in time?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. With the growing intensity of the NATO aggression, the number of people leaving Pristina and Kosovo and Metohija in general increased as well. The number was especially high between the 1st and the 15th of April, and especially high between the 6th and the 9th of April -- or the 1st and the 6th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So with the increase in intensity of the bombing, as far as I understand, the number of the people leaving increased as well.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. That area was subjected to especially intensive bombing. It seemed to us sometimes that it went on without stopping for 24 hours; incessantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, where did the people leaving town generally go? And I'm referring now to Albanians and Serbs and Montenegrins, because you told us that everybody was leaving town.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Albanians mostly went towards Macedonia, Albania, and a smaller number of them towards Montenegro. Serbs mostly went towards central Serbia, and other non-Albanians either towards central Serbia or Montenegro. I remember that the Turks went to Turkey en masse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: During NATO bombing, during NATO aggression, the health professionals working in health institutions, in view of what you did and what other state organs did, can you tell us whether you were able to work? Were the health professionals able to work?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 25th of March, in the morning, I as provisional secretary of health issued an order addressed to the heads of all health institutions in Kosovo and Metohija to ensure that all health professionals and workers continued their work and to ensure safety to those people who believed that they were endangered or that their families were endangered and to provide housing to them within the facilities of health institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that order complied with?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: This order pertaining to the management of health institution was complied with fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Under tab 11 we have some information regarding health care staff and professionals of Albanian ethnicity who remained, continued in their jobs in the hospital in Djakovica even after the beginning of the NATO aggression. Please look at tab 11. Those are Albanians, doctors who continued in their jobs in Djakovica city hospital after the beginning of the NATO aggression. Did you provide this list?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you make note of any incident that would indicate that these doctors suffered from any discrimination or any risk in their jobs?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: From what I know, they didn't. There were no such cases. There were cases, for instance, in the health care centres of Prizren and Djakovica. After the order that I issued, Albanian doctors left these health centres. Something similar happened in Gnjilane as well. In Djakovica, 95 per cent of the health care staff was Albanian, and almost all of them continued in their jobs until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Andric, during the NATO aggression, did you move around the territory of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes, every day. It was my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you come in contact with Albanians who were leaving? Let us leave aside the Serbs for the moment. Did you come in contact with the Albanians who were leaving, and was your service active on the ground?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Every day I would come in contact with hundreds of Albanians, and our services were on the ground on a daily basis, extending assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was the work of medical teams especially intensive in some particularly vulnerable areas?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had mobile medical teams, sometimes more, sometimes less, between five and ten, who worked on the border with Macedonia and near the border in the vicinity of Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you were on the ground and organising these medical teams that were extending assistance, can you tell me about the movement of the columns of Albanians leaving from -- leaving Kosovo and Metohija? Did any authorities in Serbia or in Kosovo force them to leave?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: No. They were leaving of their own accord, using their own vehicles. They travelled even in horse-drawn carts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally talk to these Albanians who were leaving the country?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: I did talk to them, dozens of them, every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you spoke to a lot of them, did you perhaps know personally some of them? What was the gist of your exchange?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: I remember, for instance, a butcher from Pristina who asked me to bring diapers for his baby.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what did you tell them when you spoke to them? You talked to a large number of people leaving.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: I was trying to convince them not to leave, to return to their homes. I was telling them that our army and our police would guarantee their safety and security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what did they say in reply? Did they do as you said or not?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Most of them did not listen to me. Some of them said they were going to take their families away from danger and then return, but most of them didn't return.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did some of them take your advice?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Very few, but some of them did. But some of those who returned I met later, after the international forces came in, and they thanked me for my advice. They told me that everyone should have stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, why were they leaving, the Albanians?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: In my opinion, the main reason was the beginning of the NATO aggression and the fear of NATO bombs. Another thing is that the Albanian population was under humungous pressure from the separatist movement, or the terrorist movement of the KLA to leave Kosovo. The KLA gave them guarantees, it seems, that they would return soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you extending any humanitarian assistance to those Albanians in addition to the medical assistance that you mentioned already? Did you give them any humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Certainly. Every day we would visit those columns of fleeing people to bring them food, diapers, milk for children. We would even provide transportation for the infirm. We would take them to the clinical centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Professor, are you aware of the reason for the KLA, as you say, pressuring the Albanians to leave Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only assume what the reason was. Their aim was to empty the territory of Kosovo from Albanians and portray that as ethnic cleansing. What I mean is that was the objective of those who were trying to persuade the population to leave. But in addition to that, there were people simply fleeing the bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You told us of your experience with people you met at the border.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like some footage shown from tab 5. 5.2 more precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Tab 11 to be an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that if the sound is going to be in Albanian, we do not have an Albanian interpreter in the English booth, so it's probably the Albanian booth who is going to read the English translation provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I note that. Let us see what happens. You saw that, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to see it now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "In Kosovo and Metohija, at the moment when some Albanians, hundred of thousands of Albanians are leaving Kosovo and Metohija, mainly Pristina, they want to pass over to the neighbouring Macedonia. Among them there are women, children, and elderly Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. people who seem tired and worn out. So only some tens of cars and hundreds of people waiting to pass over to Macedonia. As can be seen, there is no mention of tens of thousands of Albanians who wish to cross -- to leave Metohija and Kosovo, as some Western media are claiming. Among the people who, as they say, are afraid of the NATO aggression and the situation created after the attack have abandoned their homes. "Mobile ambulances were there to help them, led by Dr. Andric. These people are here to help them medical assistance to all those who need it. Among them there are representatives of the Ministry of Interior of Serbia who asked them to return to their homes because they can guarantee them full security. "Our camera shot the return of some 50 cars who, from the border checkpoint to Macedonia, pass on to Kacanik and Pristina. Our team visited the cross-border point of Macedonia -- of Yugoslavia with Albania. The situation is the same. The only difference is that the transportation of refugees is mainly through tractors. Our medical team of Red Cross of Kosovo and Metohija was there. The representatives of the Serbian Ministry of Interior are trying hard to persuade people to return back to their homes. "On the way to Pristina, we filmed that some of these people returned home. Otherwise, last night we saw about 500 cars, tractors, which were going in the direction of Pristina at the central part of Kosovo and Metohija."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do we have a date for that broadcast?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This happened on the 4th, 5th, and 6th April, 1999. This particular footage is from the 4th of April from the border crossing at Djeneral Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of this footage we were able to see you, Dr. Andric.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were talking to the refugees on the spot. One can see that the broadcast is in the Albanian language.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was this a television programme intended for Albanians because it was broadcast in Albanian?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. There is a daily programme -- there was a daily programme in Albanian, and this was part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was this broadcast on the Albanian TV programme in order to encourage people, Albanians, to stay and not leave their homes?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: The aim was to inform the entire population, including Albanians, as to what exactly was happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Nevertheless, as you said, a large number chose to leave Kosovo, whereas a smaller part took your advice and returned home. As I see in this footage, the emphasis is placed on the people who took your advice and were persuaded also by representatives of the MUP and chose to return to their homes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like this contribution to be tendered into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Andric, from your experience, from what you were able to see with your own eyes, and from what you were able to learn, were civilian facilities targeted during the bombing?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Most cities and towns were bombed daily, and many civilian targets were damaged and destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "many civilian targets," what exactly do you mean? Let us take Pristina or Djakovica, for example, or any other town in Kosovo. Is there anything in particular you remember?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: I can enumerate the targets that were hit in individual towns. In Pristina, for example, the centre of the town and the main post office, the main bus terminal, the Serbian Orthodox cemetery, the administrative building of the Jugopetrol company and their warehouse, the warehouse of the oil company Jugopetrol where a huge environmental catastrophe was caused. Then a large warehouse of commodities that spread over five hectares was hit, destroying a huge amount of goods. The deputies club in --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was the centre of Pristina bombed?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that at the beginning. The old town, the centre of Pristina, including the main post office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That will be enough.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the next video clip shown. It will illustrate our latest point.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "It coincides with --" the Albanian interpreter notes that he can't hear the video when he is speaking on the mike.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're not getting any translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Again the Albanian interpreters note that the moment we open the mike, we cannot hear the video feed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, this is the tail end of the previous video clip that hadn't ended. There were video clips 2 and 3 depicting departures from Kosovo, the presence of Mr. Andric there and his activity and the activities of other representatives of the authorities, and that was broadcast in the Albanian language in order to encourage civilians to not leave their homes, or return to their homes. And the next clip which I wanted to show is number 4, relates to the destruction that we have just heard described from Mr. Andric. That was just the tail end of the previous clip we saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes. So we are now moving to 5.4.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We returned about 500 automobiles and lorries who returned towards Pristina and the central part of Pristina and Metohija."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have seen this. That's not what I meant.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The -- no, we have seen nothing. No, we didn't see. "We came from Mitrovica. The -- we came -- we came from -- all the way from Mitrovica. Nobody ever touched us. No one said a word. "I am from Gjakove. I came from Gjakove. The parties are not in conflict with each other. That's all I wanted to say. "Have you seen anything? "No, nothing of the sort. No, nothing. "Who do you fear? "We fear the bombardment and the conflict. It's the conflict of the two parties --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was in tab 5.3, and the translation of what the people at the border are saying is in 5.3. Now I ask that tab 5.4 be played.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we move on from tab 5.3, one is bound to observe that, apart from general problems with the translation, no doubt reflecting the quality of the audio, at 6/10 was an interpretation or something said that was totally reversed from what's here in the transcript. Favourable to the accused, I would have thought, because it seems to say "I come from Djakovica" - I think this is what I heard - and it seems to say the sides are fighting but the way I heard it was no one was fighting. Can I suggest that perhaps if these clips are going to be admitted some steps be taken to tidy up the transcripts because we don't want to proceed on a false understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we are just going to ask the interpreter to listen to this particular part again, because you are right. I did hear what you said. So let us have it clarified. Have that tape replayed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson. Mr. Robinson. My transcript, which I have before me now in the Serbian language, I don't speak Albanian, but the way it's been translated, this woman says, "I have arrived from Djakovica. The sides are fighting. I am not involved with them in any way. I just want to get away until the situation calms down. When things calm down, we will live together again." And then the reporter says, "Did you face any obstacles, hindrances, problems during your journey?" And she says, "No, none at all." This is what it says here. It doesn't say what Mr. Nice said, "The sides are fighting."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the Albanian interpreter in the booth translated it a bit differently. That is why we are asking some clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We heard the same thing as Mr. Nice. But there is another way that we could deal with it. We could have a translation done.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Robinson, sir, I heard the sound. I speak Albanian quite well. When this woman is speaking of the NATO bombing, the interpreter said "the sides in the conflict." He's not saying NATO. The woman is being asked about NATO and the interpreter is again saying "the sides in the conflict."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Andric speaks Albanian, so it isn't hard for him to check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us proceed. Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will have the tape played again and have it interpreted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is tab 5.3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 5.3. Let's play it again. I don't know whether that part alone can be played. It's 6/10, 6/10, the Albanian woman speaking.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Everybody is afraid of the NATO bombing, all the world. I have come from Mitrovica. Nobody said anything to us. I have seen some 20 buses with people. "I come from Gjakove, because the sides are -- are in a conflict between them. I have no business with them, that's why I had to leave. No, nobody said anything to us. Nobody prevented us."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Stop the tape. That clarifies it. Continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Andric, at the beginning of this clip, the first man says, as far as I can see from the transcript, "We are going to Albania. We are afraid." The journalists ask, "Who are you afraid of?" And he says, "Of the shelling, because of the NATO shelling." The second Albanian man intervenes, he says, "We're afraid of the bombing, of the shelling.
