We're very afraid. Because of the situation, we're going to Albania." The reporter says, "Have you come across any obstacles in your journey here?" Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. And the second Albanian man says, "No, a little here and there, generally speaking no," and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is shown here, does this accord with your knowledge, Mr. Andric, as to the reasons for people fleeing Kosovo, and what was the attitude of the authorities toward them?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Precisely so. This is what I said before. Most of them said they were fleeing because they were afraid of the NATO bombing, and also they said they had had no problems with the authorities along the way or even before they set out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before that, I asked you about the bombing of towns in Kosovo and Metohija. Now I ask that tab 5.4 be played, and I will ask you to explain.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "I was asleep. I was asleep, and I heard a sound and then a shell fell. Then a burst of gunfire and I tried to get out. A board fell on me. When I moved it, my wife asked me if I was alive. I said I was, but I couldn't move. There was mortar all over the children, there were bricks everywhere, and it was very difficult to remove all this. And then I went to save the geese, Bosko and Jela. "It's just refugees who live in this village? "Yes, just refugees from Krajina. "How many people, approximately? "About 100 or 120, two or three more or less. "Did you hear several explosions or just one? "I heard a round. There were maybe ten bursts. Suddenly there was an explosion and everything fell on top of me. There was terrible noise everywhere. It was all over in a couple of seconds. I could hear it falling on us. And then we started moaning. "Were there many wounded or killed? "Yes, there are two or three bodies, two of women and two men. I don't know of anything else. "There were people who are wounded. My husband was wounded. My son was wounded."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Andric, this is a clip of the refugee centre that was bombed.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did you know about it?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: This is a refugee centre called Meja. It had 26 houses that had been constructed for Serbs expelled from the Republic of Croatia. In early May 1999 NATO shelled that settlement, that centre, and four persons were killed, several dozen were wounded, the Volarevic brothers from Benkovci and the Ilkic [phoen] mother and daughter from Knin were killed as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any military facilities nearby?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: No. This was simply a refugee centre for refugees from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this clip into evidence and ask that tab 5.5 be played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Tab 5.3 as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there a date for this incident? Professor, do you have the date for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure whether it was the 3rd of May or the 5th of May. I'm not absolutely sure, but it was in early May 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the centre of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the next clip. Could you stop it please? Wait a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In tab 5.5, when I viewed it in prison with you, I had the impression you could also see residential buildings that had been destroyed. Was this in another tab or did this somehow go missing from this tab?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Well, this is the shortest tab.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain what this is about?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: This is part of the very centre of Pristina, which was destroyed by NATO bombing in the night between the 6th and 7th of April, 1999, or to be more precise, on the 7th of April, early in the morning, at ten past one a.m. The very centre of Pristina was bombed and two streets, Njegoseva and Zanatska street were razed to the ground; all the residential buildings there, the main post office was severely damaged, and in this attack by the NATO Air Force, 16 citizens were killed and dozens were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You went to the spot at that time; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I live very close to that part of the town, I went with my son and his friends to the scene of these events, hoping to help those who had been injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know anyone who was killed at the time?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. My mother-in-law was killed in her own house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was her residential building destroyed?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes, completely, as were all the other residential buildings in those two streets, Zanatska street and Njegoseva street.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Your mother-in-law was killed. Her house was destroyed. What was her name?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Zlatinka Rankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the houses of some other people were also destroyed. Do you know the names of other people whose houses were hit and who were killed? You said that 16 people were killed?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember a Turkish family. Mesut Gashi was a neighbour of my mother-in-law's, and he remained buried under the rubble of his house with four children and his mother and his wife. That house caught fire, and through superhuman efforts we managed to save his mother and the youngest child. He, with his wife and three daughters, although he was alive and helping, they burnt in that house. They were burnt to death.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the next video clip. And I tender this one into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Previously -- very well, let's see this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is tab 5.7. Meja and Bistrazin near Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "I came from Krushe. When we arrived in Krushe a plane bombed us but didn't hit us. It hit the ground on the other side. When we reached this place, the bomb fell on the ground. We reached this place, we were here with the tractor. My daughter died. She was 22 years old. Was hit on the arm and in the ear. There were some wounded children, wounded women, and four men who were killed. They were hit in their legs. And then the truck came. I stayed with my daughter-in-law and three small children here to wait for my neighbours. They still haven't arrived from Djakovica in the tractor. We have no transport, and we have small children. My head was injured, and it's hard for me to walk. "And how many people are dead? "About ten, including children, men, my daughter and the women. Two women from the village of Smonica were killed on a tractor and their three sons, young quite also. And two men, Ferat Sejda from Kosara and Imer Shabani from Batusa were also killed. I know that because I was here, and there are many injured truckloads. "How many shells were fired at you? "Three from over there. See the asphalt road where it is damaged? And then over on that side. I stayed here. "Who was shooting at you? "A plane. "Do you know whose planes? "NATO's. There were many planes in the air."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Andric, this was the footage under tab 5.7.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gentlemen, you have the transcript of the words uttered by the Albanian man. You have it in English. This is the place called Bistrazin. Did they ever establish the total number of casualties? What happened there?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: NATO planes bombed a column of internally displaced Albanians who were on their way home, starting at 2.00 p.m. on the 14th of April, 1999. Throughout the following hour they bombed them on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you go to the site?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: I was at the site 15 minutes before the bombing started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: I went to Prizren, because I had to get three buses in order to transport the people with whom I had talked and had convinced them to go back to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And while you went to Prizren, the column was bombed?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I arrived at Prizren, the column was bombed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did you establish?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: The health teams from Djakovica and Prizren went to the site immediately. In that place called Meja and the place called Bistrazin, 87 civilians were killed on the spot, and 28 were killed either during the transport or in the hospitals in Djakovica and Prizren. Over 100 civilians were injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: These were all Albanians in that column, the people returning or were they leaving Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Some of them were on their way to Albania, and some were on their way back home, and these are precisely the people that I was supposed to transport in the buses. Most of them did not have any transportation and I was supposed to ensure bus transportation for them to their homes. Some people were in their tractors on their way to Albania, and when the first bomb fell, they returned to Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I apologise, but there's a problem with tab 5. I remember the houses that were destroyed. There's also tab 5.6, which was provided in a CD format, but in addition to that I have photographs of the houses that had been destroyed and that Dr. Andric spoke about that, in the centre of Pristina. So I ask that they be placed on the ELMO. These are the photographs under tab 5.6. As far as I understood it, the technical booth has these photographs in a CD format.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let them be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just briefly, please. I think that Dr. Andric has these photographs, so he can place his photographs on the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. ELMO. His photographs are better than mine because they're in colour and mine are black and white.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. These are the photographs of the post office destroyed in Pristina. Behind that you can see the bank building, and next to it is the building in which my mother-in-law was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please show us the house of your mother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What can we see in the next photograph?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: The next photograph is quite similar. It depicts the post office and the area that was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: And now the third photograph, which also shows the destroyed residential buildings.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I ask that tab 5.6 be exhibited as well, including tab 5.7, which we just saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tab 5.6, yes. And tab 5.7, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The footage that we saw under tab 5.7 showing how the column of Albanian refugees was targeted, you told us that there were 105 dead persons.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You mentioned Djakovica and the Djakovica hospital where the Albanian doctors remained working until the end of the war. Was the hospital damaged during the NATO aggression?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. During the NATO aggression the hospital was damaged four times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the extent of the damage? Was it possible to use the building or was perhaps some part of the building uninhabitable?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. A part of it was uninhabitable. The operation theatre, the surgical theatre could not be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I understood it, it wasn't a direct hit. The area next to the hospital was hit.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't hit directly, but it was damaged four times because next to it was the barracks that had been deserted four years before the war, and that was actually the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. During the aggression, did you go to Djakovica; and if so, what did you do there?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. I went to Djakovica several times. I remember the 14th of April, which is precisely the day when the column of refugees in Bistrazin was hit. I went to Djakovica because I wanted to visit the hospital and visit the patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember any specifics about that visit?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember talking to Albanian doctors. There were mostly Albanian doctors there. As I told you, 95 per cent of the employees there were Albanians. I remember that out of 13 wards, only seven were in operation. And on at that day, the 14th of April, 1999, the hospital had 157 patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then after that you went to Prizren?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. I went to Prizren to get the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you told us what happened afterwards. And immediately after that, this event took place, the bombing of the refugee column in the course of which 105 civilians were killed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let us see the next clip which deals with the Djakovica hospital, and it's under tab 5.8.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Stay quiet. Stay quiet. Don't move. It's okay. It's okay. "Djakovica municipality. "Nearly all of your children who came with you were injured. "Yes, that's right. My relatives have been wounded or killed. My wife's sister, who was 22, died now and she left behind a young son. My five sons are here. All of them have been wounded. We noticed the round. We were lucky. When we came to Pec, I don't know how many bombs fell. In two tractors five people were killed. They're all here. "All in one place. "Yes, just in one place, in Pec, where the brick factory is or whatever it's called. "Are your children seriously injured? "The youngest one was wounded in the chest and legs and also there is a wound between his shoulders, a serious wound. And then two sons, then there's a person there hit, injured in the head, and a woman with an injury on her neck. "What did the doctors say? "The doctors helped a lot. They helped a lot certainly. "They say that the United States wants to protect the Albanian people. Is that how they're protecting the women and the children? "Yes. You can see it for yourself. "They shoot two or three times and then they hit me on the arm. There was a neighbour next to me came and drove me here in his car. The others stayed there, and the others, the police went and brought them here."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the next clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, let us stop the tape.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I ask that tab 5.8, depicting the situation in the Djakovica hospital, also be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Under tab 5.9, you will see that the document there is translated into English. These are two written statements given by Cuni Zoja, the first one, and the second one was given by Sulja Ljabinot. Yes. I apologise, I misread the last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For good order and lest it be thought that I am agreeing for all later witnesses to a course of action being taken with respect of this witness, statements of this kind, witness statements, would normally have to be either admitted under 92 bis or 89(F), otherwise they would be inadmissible. Now, the accused might usefully remind himself that there are provisions for making material like this available through the Rules of the Court. I'm anxious to take no time with any technical objection today -- not technical objection, with any objection today, and would ask that for the time being these are marked for identification only and their status reviewed at the end of all the evidence. I don't -- I don't resist their being read since they've now been made available to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What you're saying is that the witness should be called, or 92 bis or --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the moment I don't. I simply say let's at least recognise that what's happening here is well outside our normal Rules of Procedure. If the Chamber de bene esse wishes to read these statements, I'm not going to stand in the way by any form of objection, but can we put back to the end of the evidence of this witness the question whether they stand marked for identification or whether they are produced. I have a reason for doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you're saying you will review the status at the end of the day and consider whether you agree with it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We won't admit it now. Mr. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, before you rule on Mr. Nice's objection, let me tell you that these statements, as you can see from them, are dealing with precisely that day, the 14th of April, 1999. And the witness who is before us now was on site. We saw the footage, we saw the hospital, and the witness obtained the statements which describe the events of that date. So this is not something that is not directly linked to the evidence of this witness. On the contrary, it is directly linked because he was there on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We acknowledge the linkage. It's just the question of admission. But what Mr. Nice was referring to were the modalities open to you under the Rules of Evidence, and you might consider utilising those modalities for statements of this kind. We will come back to this later. It's now 2.00, when we said we would break. We will now adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 24th day of February, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.
